So the ICU years. This is Mission Trail Regional Medical Center in San Antonio, the main hospital in the Mission Trail Health system. I transferred from med-surg up to the MICU in 2016, I think it was June, right after I finished the ICU internship they had for internal transfers. It's a 24-bed medical ICU, a lot of septic patients, respiratory failure, DKA, GI bleeds, overdoses, a lot of our patients came straight from the ED. Ratios were one to two, sometimes one to one if someone was really unstable or on CRRT.

The first year was rough honestly. I went from six patients to two and it felt like more work, not less, because everything is drips and titrations and you're in the room constantly. But I loved it. I loved knowing everything about my two people.

I got charge in the spring of 2018. I remember because it was right after my birthday and it was maybe six months after Epic went live, so everyone was still complaining about Epic. I started as relief charge on nights and then moved to days. Charge on a 24-bed unit means you're doing the assignments, the bed flow with the house supervisor, who's getting the next admit, rapid responses, codes, dealing with families who are upset, dealing with doctors who are upset. We had a staff of about 45 nurses between days and nights, plus techs. I did the schedule requests for a while too, which nobody wants to do.

The project I always talk about is the sepsis bundle. That was 2019. Our compliance with the sepsis bundle, the SEP-1 stuff, lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within the hour, fluids, the repeat lactate, was bad. Like 58 percent when we started. Quality kept sending us these reports and everyone just kind of shrugged. So me and our clinical nurse specialist, she was amazing, we co-led a project on it. I did the bedside side of it and she did the committee side, if that makes sense.

What we did. We made it nurse-driven, so the nurse could start the sepsis screening on admission and every four hours without waiting for the resident to notice. We worked with the informatics team to change the Epic sepsis screening alert, the best practice advisory, because it was firing all the time and everyone was clicking through it. We got it to fire less and actually mean something. I made a little laminated bundle card for every room. And I audited charts myself, I think twenty charts a month, and posted the results in the break room by shift, which people hated at first, and then nights started trying to beat days, so that was fun.

By the end, I think it was about nine months, we were at 86 percent compliance. 58 to 86. That number I'm sure about because I had to present it at the nursing quality council. And honestly I think we basically cut sepsis deaths in half on our unit. I mean, nobody ever showed us actual mortality numbers, quality only reported compliance to us, but it felt like it. Patients were getting antibiotics faster, that I know.

Other stuff in the ICU. I was on the unit's code team rotation. I did the CRRT training and became one of the CRRT resource nurses, there were maybe five of us. I precepted ICU transfers, I don't remember how many, a few. I got my CCRN in 2017, I want to say. Yeah, 2017, before charge.

The hard part was the end. COVID hit in March 2020 and the MICU became a COVID unit basically overnight. We were short constantly, people were leaving for travel jobs making three times what we made, and as charge I was the one telling people they had to take three vented patients. I did that until June 2020 and then I left to go travel myself, which, I know. I felt guilty about it for a long time. But that's the next part.

Anyway the thing I liked most about charge, if I'm honest, wasn't the clinical stuff. It was the puzzle. Who goes where, which nurse is good with which family, how do we get the bed upstairs cleaned before the ED calls again. I didn't know that's what I liked until way later.
